Subject: Dedicated pool - clarification on inflight guarantees and eviction behavior

Hi Grace and Ben,

Thanks again for the demo last week. As we get closer to finalizing the reserved GPU commitment for FastLedger (DL-8742), our engineering and ops teams asked for a few clarifications so we can lock the procurement timeline:

1) Eviction/preemption: if Redwood needs to reclaim capacity during a regional outage or maintenance event, how are inflight requests handled? Do you surface partial responses, or is an explicit 503 returned? Is there an automatic retry to another compatible pool?

2) Inflight guarantees: can you confirm the per-request inflight concurrency and tail-latency guarantees for a reserved pool of 32x A100-equivalent GPUs under steady-state and 2x burst? We need this to size our client-side timeouts.

3) Queueing behavior: when concurrency exceeds the pool, is there client-side backpressure (429) or does Redwood queue requests server-side up to a window? If queued, what are typical max queue durations and observability hooks we can rely on (metrics/logs/trace ids)?

I've attached our initial SLA questionnaire with the sections highlighted. If it's easier, happy to do a short working session with your SREs this week.

Best,
Samir
Senior Infrastructure Engineer
FastLedger

Subject: Re: Dedicated pool - clarification on inflight guarantees and eviction behavior

Thanks Samir — clear asks. Looping in David (SRE) and Lauren (Legal/Contracts) so we can give combined operational + contractual answers.

High level answers up front:
- Eviction: for Reserved (non-preemptible) pools, we do not evict active workers for routine maintenance; instead we prefer node drain with connection handoff and KV cache warmup to minimize 503s. In extreme regions/outages we have an ordered fallback to compatible pools (same model quantization + region policy). We will provide a playbook excerpt showing the decision tree.

- Inflight guarantees: we expose a per-request latency SLO and a per-pool concurrency cap. For a 32-GPU reserved pool we expect steady-state throughput of ~1.9M tokens/sec (model dependent) and a 99.9th percentile tail-latency target of 450ms for typical 256-token requests under nominal load. We will provide a quantified table in the addendum — that number can be tightened in the contract if you opt for dedicated isolation lanes.

- Queueing: by default Redwood uses server-side short-window queuing (up to ~30s in extreme backlogs) with circuit-breaker responses (429) when queue depth exceeds configured headroom. We provide token-level tracing and a headroom metric so you can trigger client-side backoff.

I've attached an internal draft of an eviction/playbook fragment to start the negotiation. David — can you add the technical snippet for queue-shaping and preemption signals? Lauren — can you confirm whether we should surface a carveout clause for FastLedger's reserved-node contract?

Cheers,
Grace
Director, Solutions
Redwood Inference

Hi team — adding the technical detail Samir asked for. Excerpt from the runtime playbook below (trimmed):

--- runtime excerpt ---
1) Drain vs Evict
   - Maintenance: nodes are drained; new requests routed to warm workers where possible. Active KV cache is streamed to replacement workers when warmup completes. Returns: graceful 200 responses; no forced 503 for in-flight tokens.
   - Emergency outage: if node network is disrupted and handoff can't complete within the fail-window (currently 12s by config), we mark in-flight contexts as failed and return 503 to callers; automatic retry policy attempts recovery to fallback pool for idempotent requests.

2) Queue shaping
   - Each reserved pool exposes a headroom metric (tokens/sec capacity left) and a server-side windowed FIFO queue. Default max queuing time is 30s; we emit metrics: queue_depth, queue_time_p95, headroom_pct, preemption_signal_time.
   - If queue_time_p95 exceeds your client timeout, Redwood will start shedding excess with 429 to prevent cascading latency spikes. We can tune the window per-customer in contract.

3) Preemption signals and observability
   - Preemption starts with a 60s advisory webhook (fastledger/eviction-advisory), then a 12s forced-evict window for non-isolated pools. For isolation-lane customers, that advisory becomes a contractual prohibition (no automatic evictions except for force majeure).

I attached a quick diagram that shows the request path and where traces/logs are emitted. Happy to run a one-hour walkthrough with your infra leads.

-David
Senior SRE, Runtime
Redwood Inference
